title: rhino-core: plan-and-grill, verify and pr-story

story: Dana, a teammate from the backend team, is asked to review the frontend pull request for RH-1234, the ticket that adds a "No projects yet" card to an empty projects table. The description says: "Added an empty state to the projects table. All tests pass. Checked it locally and it looks good."

She does not know the frontend well, and nothing in the description tells her what "checked" means. Was a filter with no results tested, or only the empty workgroup? At which screen width? She pulls the branch, starts the app, makes test data and clicks around for forty minutes, doing the checking again herself. The work may have been perfect. The description just gave her claims instead of proof.
hook.question: How do the plan, the checking and the pull request connect, so a reviewer from another team can see in a few minutes that each promise was kept?

p: rhino-core, the plugin every engineer and every agent gets, starts with three skills, one for each moment of a change. plan-and-grill is used before any code: it decides whether to ask the requester questions first (to grill them), then writes a one-screen plan. verify is used before anyone says "done": it runs the checks and records proof. pr-story is used when the pull request is opened: it writes the description in fixed headings.

Each skill is useful alone, but the real value is the thread between them, and the thread is the check. A check is one promise about what the user will see, written in the plan with a short label such as C1, and with the kind of proof it needs. verify records proof under the same label, and pr-story lists every label with its result. A reviewer can then follow each promise from the plan to its proof, and a missing check is as easy to see as a missing line in a list.

read.h: The plan names the proof before the code
p: The plan starts with the definition of done: one or two sentences, in the user's words, about what is true when the work is finished. Then come three to five checks, at least one of them an edge case, which is the unusual input that breaks careless code. For RH-1234 the edge case is a workgroup with 1,000 projects, where the first page must still show 25 rows.

Each check names its proof now, before any code exists. A flow gets a short video, a layout gets screenshots at 760 and 1440 pixels (our narrowest and widest supported widths), and an API call or a test run gets text output. Choosing the proof first matters for an honest reason: after the work is done, it is tempting to show whatever looks good, and a screenshot of the happy path proves nothing about the filter case.

notes.text: The definition of done, in the user's words.
Each check has a label that travels into the proof and the pull request.
A flow: something moves on screen, so a still picture cannot prove it.
The edge case. Its proof is a test's text output.

deeper.h: Go deeper: ask first, or plan now?
p: The grill half of plan-and-grill decides whether the plan can be written at all. A big ticket, a ticket that spans teams, or one where two readings would lead to different code gets questions to the requester first. The signs are concrete: no example, a vague verb such as "improve" or "support", a screen with no states, a change to an API other teams use. A small, clear fix such as a typo goes straight to the plan, because five questions about a typo waste a day.
Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, uses the same skill and posts the same plan format on Jira and in Slack. So when a person approves Nova's plan, they read exactly the shape they write themselves.

read.h: verify keeps the label on the proof
p: verify starts from the area's verify command (lint, type checks and the related tests), then checks what the user would see, on seed data (fake data made for testing) and never on real customer data. For each check it records the command, pass or fail, and the proof the plan named, labelled with the check: C1-760.png, C1-1440.png, a 12-second no-results.mp4 for C2, the test output for C3.

Two parts of verify keep the proof honest. A failing check belongs to the change until main's latest run shows the same failure, and the answer is to fix the code, not to skip or loosen the check. And a new check must be shown to fail at least once, by breaking the change on purpose; that habit has a lesson of its own at the end of this part.

read.h: pr-story puts the proof where the reviewer looks
p: pr-story writes every pull request description in the same headings, in the same order: What changes, Why, How it was checked, What was not checked and why, Risk and rollback, Where to look first. The fixed order is for the reviewer: after two pull requests they know where the answer to each question lives. The part above the fold stays under about 300 words, and long output goes into a link or a folded details block. The title follows one rule too: [FE] RH-1234: and what changes for the user.

How it was checked has one line per check from the plan, with its label, its result and its proof. What was not checked is just as important, because a gap that is written down is a decision the reviewer can agree with, while a gap that is not written down looks like a check that passed. Below is the same pull request written this way; the backend reviewer can check it in a few minutes, because every promise in the plan points to its proof.

code.file: the PR description, written with pr-story
code.text:
[FE] RH-1234: Empty projects table shows a No projects yet card

## What changes
A workgroup with no projects now shows a "No projects yet" card instead of an empty grid.

## Why
RH-1234. The table rendered its grid even with zero rows (ProjectsTable.tsx:48).

## How it was checked
- C1 empty card: pass. Screenshots at 760 and 1440: empty-760.png, empty-1440.png
- C2 filter with no match: pass. Video, 12 s: no-results.mp4
- C3 1,000 projects: pass. `npx vitest run ProjectsTable` shows "first page renders 25 rows"

## What was not checked, and why
Dark mode, because the card uses existing design-system colours only.

## Risk and rollback
Low. Revert the PR; no data or API change.

## Where to look first
ProjectsTable.tsx and its new story, ProjectsTable.stories.tsx.

notes.text: The title rule: [FE] or [BE], the ticket, and what changes for the user.
The root cause in one line, with file and line.
One line per check from the plan: label, result, and the proof the plan asked for.
A gap written down is a decision the reviewer can agree with.

deeper.h: Go deeper: one template, not two
p: fcp already had a pull request template with headings such as Summary of Changes and Testing Performed. Adding a second template for agents would give reviewers two shapes to learn, so the existing one moves to pr-story's headings instead: Summary of Changes becomes What changes, References becomes Why, Testing Performed becomes How it was checked plus What was not checked, and Implementation Details becomes Where to look first. People and agents then fill in the same page.

Media follows the change, not habit: a short video for a flow, before and after screenshots at 760 and 1440 for layout, a diagram for a changed flow between services, text for API calls and migrations, and nothing for a refactor that changes nothing visible. Never pictures of code or logs, which a reviewer cannot search or copy, and never real data.

lab.title: Trace every check to its proof
lab.goal: Run a small checker that follows each check of a plan into a pull request description, then write the description for RH-1234 so every check has a result and the proof the plan promised.

guess.q: A plan has three checks. The pull request says "All tests pass. Checked it locally and it looks good." How many of the three checks can a reviewer trace to proof?

options.text: All three, because all tests pass
options.why: "All tests pass" does not say which tests, so the reviewer cannot tell whether the filter case or the 1,000-projects case was covered.
No line names a check, a result or a piece of proof. The reviewer has to check everything again.
Even the main check has no proof attached: no screenshot, no width, no test output.

follow.say: Write the plan's checks for RH-1234, the same shape plan-and-grill writes, each with the kind of proof it needs.

Write the checker. It reads the plan and a pull request description, checks the headings and their order, and looks for one line for each check, with a result and the promised proof. A reviewer does this in their head; the script makes it visible.
Run it on the description from the story, so you see what claims look like to a reviewer.
follow.do:
cat > pr.md <<'EOF'
[FE] RH-1234: Empty projects table shows a No projects yet card

## Summary of Changes
Added an empty state to the projects table.

## Testing Performed
All tests pass. Checked it locally and it looks good.
EOF
node trace.mjs plan.json pr.md
follow.see:
✘ headings
   want: What changes / Why / How it was checked / What was not checked, and why / Risk and rollback / Where to look first
   have: Summary of Changes / Testing Performed
✘ C1 empty workgroup shows the No projects yet card: no line in How it was checked
✘ C2 a filter with no match shows No results, not the empty card: no line in How it was checked
✘ C3 1,000 projects: the first page shows 25 rows: no line in How it was checked

4 problem(s): a reviewer cannot trace every check to its proof

lab.build: Rewrite pr.md the way pr-story would: the title, the six headings in order, and under How it was checked one line for each check, with its label (C1, C2, C3), pass or fail, and the proof the plan named (screenshots at 760 and 1440 for C1, a video for C2, the test command in backticks for C3). Add one honest line under What was not checked, and why. Run node trace.mjs plan.json pr.md until it prints Every check in the plan has a result and the proof it promised. Then check the word count above the fold with wc -w pr.md: it should be well under 300.
checks: node trace.mjs plan.json pr.md prints ✔ for the headings and for C1, C2 and C3, and exits with code 0.
Each line under How it was checked starts from the plan's label, so a reviewer can match it to the plan.
What was not checked names something real and says why, instead of being empty.
The description is under 300 words (wc -w pr.md).

lab.fix: A teammate was in a hurry and replaced the video for C2 with a screenshot: "C2 filter with no match: pass. Screenshot: no-results.png". Make that change and run the checker: it says ✘ C2 … the plan asked for video as proof. Explain to the teammate why one picture cannot prove a filter flow, and put the video back (or, if the video truly cannot be made, move C2 to What was not checked, and why, and say so).
explain: Why does each check get a label in the plan, and where does that label appear again?
Why is the kind of proof chosen in the plan, before the code is written?
What does a reviewer learn from What was not checked, and why, that a list of passed checks cannot tell them?
lab.done: Your pr.md passes the checker, stays under 300 words, and you can explain why the C2 screenshot was not enough.

check.q: Why does each check in the plan carry a label such as C2 that appears again in the proof file names and in the pull request?

options.text: So the reviewer can follow each promise from the plan to its result and proof, and see at once when one is missing
options.why: The label is the thread. Without it, the reviewer has to guess which test or screenshot belongs to which promise.

options.text: Because Jira requires numbered checks before a ticket can move
options.why: Jira knows nothing about our checks. The label is for the people reading the work.

options.text: So the tests run in the order of the labels
options.why: The labels do not change how tests run. They connect the plan, the proof and the description.

check.q: Why does the plan decide the kind of proof for each check before any code is written?

options.text: Because recording a video takes longer than writing code
options.why: Time is not the reason. The reason is what the proof is allowed to show.

options.text: Because after the work is done, it is tempting to show whatever looks good, such as a screenshot of the easy case
options.why: Choosing proof first ties it to the promise. The filter check needs a video of the filter, not a picture of the happy path.

options.text: Because verify cannot record proof that the plan did not list
options.why: verify can record anything. The plan sets what the reviewer should expect, so a weaker proof stands out.

check.q: A pull request lists three passed checks and leaves What was not checked, and why empty. The author skipped dark mode on purpose. What is the problem?

options.text: None: the empty section means everything was checked
options.why: That is exactly what the reviewer will believe, and it is not true.

options.text: The pull request is too short, because pr-story wants more words
options.why: pr-story wants fewer words, under about 300 above the fold. The problem is a missing fact, not length.

options.text: The reviewer reads the silence as "checked"; a gap written down is a decision they can agree or disagree with
options.why: Saying "dark mode not checked, because the card uses existing colours" lets the reviewer judge the risk instead of missing it.

p: plan-and-grill, verify and pr-story are the first skills of rhino-core in RhinoHealth/claude-plugins, each with a short SKILL.md, references/ files for depth, and three or four eval cases. Nova's readiness check and grill step use plan-and-grill and post the same plan format to Jira and Slack; Nova's PR judge reads descriptions written with pr-story.

verify's per-area reference starts from npm run verify in frontend/ and poe verify for cloud, client and sdk, with the older commands (lint, check-types, vitest on related files; the backend unit test script) until those scripts exist. One line in fcp's frontend/AGENTS.md and root CLAUDE.md points to verify. fcp's .github/pull_request_template.md moves to pr-story's headings.

tickets.why: plan-and-grill: ask first or plan now, then a one-screen plan with checks, proof, estimate, risks and scope.
verify: the area's command, proof per check, honest failures, and the pointer in AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md.
pr-story: the fixed headings, the media guide, the ticket comment format, and fcp's PR template.

words.plain: One or two sentences, in the user's words, about what is true when the work is finished.
One labelled promise about what the user will see, with the kind of proof it needs.
An unusual input that breaks careless code, such as a workgroup with 1,000 projects.
What shows a check ran and passed: a short video, screenshots at 760 and 1440, or text output.
Asking the requester sharp questions before planning, for big or vague tickets only.

review.q: From memory, write pr-story's six headings in order.
review.a: What changes; Why; How it was checked; What was not checked, and why; Risk and rollback; Where to look first.

review.q: A plan's check says "the card looks right". What is wrong with it, and how would you rewrite it?
review.a: It names no situation and no proof. Rewrite it as a labelled check about what the user sees in one case, with its proof: "C1 an empty workgroup shows the No projects yet card; screenshots at 760 and 1440".

remember: Give every check a label and its proof in the plan, keep the label on the proof, and list each one in the pull request: the reviewer follows the thread instead of checking everything again.
